title: Progressive breathlessness despite repeated treatment for a COPD exacerbation
purpose: Assess progressive hypoxaemia, exposures and uncertain early lung findings.
role: patient and record system in the early communicative phase
decision_point: Early admission, while requiring 2 L/min nasal-cannula oxygen and before day-3 BAL or later antibody results, ventilation, transfer and ECMO. The early CT and admission laboratory/examination packet are requestable experimental releases; no unsupplied result-return times are asserted.
opening: A 65-year-old woman with COPD has one month of worsening breathlessness after cough and wheeze. She has not improved with outpatient treatment and now needs supplemental oxygen at admission.
task: Audience: a clinician. Use 180-260 words in English. Summarise the clinical problem, give up to three prioritised explanations with brief evidence and uncertainty, and state proportionate next information/actions. Use only information actually supplied. Do not invent findings, measured values, doses or probabilities. Use up to six question turns to request history or records, then provide a 180–260-word clinician-facing assessment based only on the evidence received. Obtain exposure and treatment history, assess the respiratory risk and develop a proportionate differential. This is the early communicative phase; do not use the later ventilated course or later discordant specialist tests as if already known. Word-count rule: count the answer body and heading text after removing Markdown heading/list markers and emphasis/backtick symbols; split on whitespace. Hyphenated expressions count as one word. Exclude JSON only if the task explicitly excludes it. No extra tolerance is added to the stated word range.
adaptation: Published facts are paraphrased into fixed replies. The opening, task, channel assignment, question budget, candidate requirements and request-triggered release are researcher-designed. Requestability is an experimental information-release rule, not a claim about actual test ordering or turnaround time. Later outcomes and examiner-only reference information are not simulator evidence. Missing findings are not invented as normal. All clinical reference and essential-request choices await confirmation. This uses only omag190/PAP lines in the shared extract. The omag191/Fabry boy contributes no facts. Initial oxygen support is retained without inventing spontaneous first-person speech during later ventilation. D3c is excluded because it is absent from the allowed snapshot.
hidden: Day-3 BAL cell differential, appearance, stains and cultures; subsequent anti-GM-CSF antibody results; later CT; treatment escalation/response; repeated BAL, whole-lung lavage and PAS findings; intubation, ECMO, infections, death and post-mortem pathology. An order for serology is not a positive result. The source leaves the contributors to acute lung injury uncertain even retrospectively.

facts.text: My breathing has worsened over about a month. It began with cough and wheeze; later I developed fever, chills and general weakness.
I smoke tobacco daily. I recently resumed vaping after having stopped seven years earlier.

No relevant occupational or environmental exposure, medication-related pulmonary risk factor, diabetes or other known cause of immunocompromise was reported. Details beyond those documented categories are not supplied.
The recorded background includes COPD and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease.
For presumed COPD exacerbation I received two courses of steroids; the second was combined with ten days of doxycycline. I did not improve clinically.

At admission she had hypoxaemic respiratory failure requiring 2 L/min oxygen by nasal cannula. Examination found diffuse basal crackles, minimal late expiratory wheeze and poor air movement. No numerical saturation or arterial blood gas is supplied in the saved presentation paragraph.

White-cell count was reported as 18,000 and procalcitonin negative. COVID-19 and influenza tests were negative. Early chest CT showed extensive bilateral ground-glass opacities. The later serological results and BAL are outside this early packet.

reference:
This is progressive respiratory illness with an oxygen requirement despite treatment for presumed COPD exacerbation. Hypoxaemic respiratory failure warrants active inpatient assessment, oxygen and repeated monitoring, with prompt respiratory or critical-care escalation if support needs increase. Establish current saturation, work of breathing, haemodynamics and blood gas where indicated; numerical values not supplied in the packet must not be invented.

Clarify smoking and the recent return to vaping, other inhalational or occupational exposures, medication risks and the timing of outpatient therapy. If received, failure to improve after two steroid courses and doxycycline, basal crackles and extensive bilateral ground-glass change argue for reassessing the initial label. Infection, inhalational injury, inflammatory or interstitial disease and other diffuse alveolar processes remain possibilities, alongside relevant cardiopulmonary alternatives. Negative viral tests or procalcitonin alone do not eliminate every infection.

Vaping exposure supplies a plausible clue but does not prove causation. The early CT pattern is not diagnostic of a specific proteinosis or injury mechanism. Target subsequent investigations to unresolved alternatives and clinical stability, including specialist consideration of lavage or serology where appropriate. At this decision point those tests have not returned. Do not import a later elevated antibody, inconclusive lavage, post-mortem result, response to treatment or death into the initial synthesis. Even the retrospective report leaves the relative contributors to acute lung injury unresolved.

answer:
**Clinical Problem**

A 65-year-old woman with COPD presents with one month of progressive dyspnoea, cough, wheeze, fever and chills, unresponsive to two steroid courses and doxycycline. She requires 2 L/min nasal-cannula oxygen at admission. Examination shows diffuse basal crackles, poor air movement and minimal late expiratory wheeze. WBC is 18,000; procalcitonin is negative; respiratory viral tests are negative. Early CT shows extensive bilateral ground-glass opacities.

**Differential**

- Eosinophilic or hypersensitivity pneumonitis – Bilateral GGOs with fever, unresponsiveness to antibiotics and steroids, and recent vaping resumption raise this possibility. However, the interval between vaping resumption and symptom onset is unknown, and no eosinophil count or specific exposure history is supplied.
- Atypical or opportunistic infection – Leukocytosis with negative procalcitonin and negative common viral tests is discordant; an atypical bacterial, fungal or viral aetiology cannot be excluded. No travel, sick-contact or immunocompromise history is documented.
- COPD exacerbation with superimposed process – Basal crackles and poor air movement are consistent with her known COPD, but the degree of bilateral GGO and failure to respond to steroids argue against a simple exacerbation.

**Next steps**

Obtain room-air saturation and arterial blood gas, peripheral eosinophil count, and a full medication and supplement reconciliation. Consider bronchoscopy with BAL for cytology, culture and cell differential. Review vaping product details and timing relative to symptom onset.

scores.name: Factual accuracy and groundedness
scores.reason: The submission is factually accurate throughout and grounded strictly in the supplied evidence. All stated findings trace to the actual returned information: Q1/Q5 (two steroid courses, second with ten days of doxycycline, no clinical improvement, daily tobacco smoking, resumed vaping after seven years), Q2 (fever, chills, weakness; no relevant occupational/environmental exposure reported), and Q3 (2 L/min nasal-cannula oxygen, diffuse basal crackles, minimal late expiratory wheeze, poor air movement, WBC 18,000, negative procalcitonin, negative COVID-19/influenza tests, extensive bilateral ground-glass opacities on early CT). It does not invent findings: it explicitly notes the vaping-to-symptom interval is unknown, that no eosinophil count or specific exposure history is supplied, and that travel/sick-contact/immunocompromise histories are undocumented rather than confirmed negative—matching the environment feedback constraints. The differential (eosinophilic/hypersensitivity pneumonitis, atypical/opportunistic infection, COPD exacerbation with superimposed process) is proportionate and consistent with the provisional reference points, and it avoids importing later BAL, serology, ventilation or outcome data. Next steps (room-air saturation/ABG, eosinophil count, medication reconciliation, BAL consideration, vaping product review) are appropriate and do not assert unrevealed results. The submission explicitly acknowledges uncertainty where evidence is incomplete, satisfying the score-5 anchor.

scores.name: Problem representation
scores.reason: The submission synthesises the actually supplied early-admission evidence into a focused, clinically meaningful representation: it correctly integrates the subacute progressive dyspnoea with fever/chills, failure of two steroid courses plus doxycycline, hypoxaemia on 2 L/min oxygen, examination findings, leukocytosis with negative procalcitonin and viral tests, and extensive bilateral ground-glass opacities on early CT. The differential is appropriately prioritised and evidence-linked (hypersensitivity/eosinophilic pneumonitis given vaping resumption and steroid failure; atypical/opportunistic infection given the discordant inflammatory markers; COPD exacerbation as a partial but insufficient explanation). Uncertainty is properly qualified rather than closed: the vaping-to-symptom interval is stated as unknown, no eosinophil count is available, and travel/sick-contact/immunocompromise histories are described as not documented rather than confirmed absent — consistent with the environment feedback for Q2 and Q4. It does not import later BAL, serology, ventilation or ECMO information, and its proposed next steps (ABG, eosinophil count, BAL, medication reconciliation) are proportionate and derive from identified gaps. No distortion, unjustified commitment, or unqualified consequential gap is present. This matches the Score 5 anchor: discriminating features are highlighted, hypothesis generation is guided, and unresolved limitations are made explicit.

The submission provides a focused, accurate synthesis of the evidence actually supplied at the early-admission decision point: COPD with a month of progressive dyspnoea, fever/chills, failure of two steroid courses plus doxycycline, hypoxaemia on 2 L/min, diffuse basal crackles, WBC 18,000, negative procalcitonin and viral tests, and extensive bilateral ground-glass opacities (Q1–Q3). It highlights the discriminating features — recent vaping resumption (Q1/Q4), steroid/antibiotic non-response, and the discordant leukocytosis with negative procalcitonin — and uses them to prioritise a plausible differential (hypersensitivity/eosinophilic pneumonitis, atypical/opportunistic infection, COPD exacerbation with superimposed process). Uncertainty is appropriately qualified: it notes the unknown interval between vaping resumption and symptom onset (consistent with Q4 feedback), the absence of eosinophil counts, and that histories of travel, sick contacts and immunocompromise are not documented rather than confirmed negative. It does not invoke later BAL, serology, ventilation or outcomes, and does not invent values. Next steps (room-air saturation/ABG, eosinophil count, medication reconciliation, BAL, vaping details) are proportionate and match the identified gaps. The representation integrates the important available evidence, guides hypothesis generation, and clearly flags unresolved gaps, meeting the score-5 anchor.

scores.name: Differential Diagnosis Generation
scores.reason: The submission gives a clinically plausible, prioritised differential grounded in actual supplied evidence (bilateral ground-glass opacities on early CT, fever/chills, WBC 18,000 with negative procalcitonin, negative viral tests, failure of two steroid courses plus doxycycline, and recent vaping resumption from Q1/Q4). It appropriately flags uncertainty (vaping interval unknown, no eosinophil count, incomplete exposure history) and does not import later BAL/serology findings. However, it omits an important alternative—cardiogenic pulmonary oedema/heart failure, a classic dangerous mimic of bilateral basal crackles with ground-glass opacities—despite the reference points explicitly listing 'relevant cardiopulmonary alternatives'. Vaping-associated lung injury (EVALI) is also only implicitly covered under hypersensitivity pneumonitis rather than distinctly considered. Discriminating findings are partially used (procalcitonin discordance, steroid non-response), but the breadth is incomplete and support is not fully proportionate, matching Score 3: plausible differential with incomplete prioritisation/support rather than the breadth-appropriate, mimic-attentive differential of Score 4.

scores.name: Context seeking
scores.reason: All three frozen essential requirements were met through targeted, appropriately timed interactive requests before the final assessment. R1 (exposures with timing): Q1 sought smoking history, Q2 covered occupational/environmental exposures and sick contacts, Q4 pursued vaping timing/product details, and Q5 covered new medications/supplements. R2 (course and treatment response): Q1 directly asked about outpatient steroids, antibiotics, nebulisers and response. R3 (oxygenation/severity and investigations): Q3 requested admission examination, vitals, saturation and early CT, which returned oxygen requirement, crackles, WCC, procalcitonin, COVID/influenza and bilateral ground-glass CT. Each request was accompanied by a prospectively allowed assessment note explaining how the information would affect interpretation (e.g., Q4's EVALI rationale linked to the GGO pattern, fever and treatment failure). Requests were proportionate and discriminating, prioritising high-yield data (severity and imaging) at Q3 and refining the emerging differential at Q4–Q5. Unfulfilled items (FEV1/GOLD stage, vaping product details, numerical saturation) reflect simulator limits, not inadequate requests, and an adequate request counts even when unavailable. No unnecessary information gathering was evident within the six-turn budget; no essential requirement was missed or requested too late.

scores.name: Appropriateness of expressed uncertainty
scores.reason: The submission calibrates confidence to the available early-packet evidence and distinguishes known from unknown throughout. It names specific sources of uncertainty: the unknown interval between vaping resumption and symptom onset (Q4 confirmed this is not supplied), the absent eosinophil count, the discordance of leukocytosis 18,000 with negative procalcitonin and negative viral tests (Q3), and the absence of documented travel/sick-contact/immunocompromise history (Q2). Language is appropriately graded ('raise this possibility', 'cannot be excluded', 'argue against a simple exacerbation'), avoiding false certainty while not hedging generically. It also proposes concrete next steps to reduce uncertainty (room-air saturation/ABG, eosinophil count, BAL, medication reconciliation, vaping timing). It falls short of the Score 5 anchor because it does not clearly separate established, probable, possible and unresolved conclusions into a ranked structure, and it does not fully explain the mechanism of uncertainty for each differential item. No anchor descriptions were missing, so the assessment is determinate.

scores.name: Escalation/Emergency Recognition
scores.reason: The submission recognises a serious situation (hypoxaemic respiratory failure on 2 L/min oxygen, bilateral ground-glass opacities, failure of two treatment courses) and lists investigations, but it never recommends an escalation pathway or conveys urgency. There is no statement of inpatient monitoring frequency, oxygen titration, ICU/respiratory-escalation criteria, or any timing for the proposed actions (ABG, eosinophil count, BAL are listed without urgency or a plan if support needs increase). The reference points explicitly call for active inpatient assessment with repeated monitoring and prompt respiratory/critical-care escalation if support needs increase; the submission omits this entirely. This matches Score 2: recognises that something is serious but does not recommend an appropriate escalation pathway.

scores.name: Causal Reasoning Appropriateness
scores.reason: The submission makes task-relevant causal claims grounded in the supplied evidence: it links the differential (hypersensitivity/eosinophilic pneumonitis, atypical infection, COPD exacerbation with superimposed process) to actual findings from Q1–Q3 (failure to improve after two steroid courses and doxycycline, WBC 18,000, negative procalcitonin and viral tests, bilateral ground-glass opacities, basal crackles), and it states material limitations — e.g., the vaping-to-symptom interval is unknown (per Q4 feedback), no eosinophil count is available, and negative viral/procalcitonin tests do not exclude infection. It avoids importing later BAL/serology/outcome data. It falls short of a 5 because of minor causal imprecision: listing eosinophilic pneumonitis as a leading explanation while simultaneously citing steroid unresponsiveness as supporting evidence overlooks that eosinophilic disease typically responds to steroids, and the 'atypical infection' item cites absence of documented travel/sick-contact history where those details were simply not supplied. These are small overstatements rather than unsupported assumptions, so the account is broadly sound with stated limitations — a Score 4.

D3a.name: Problem representation

anchors.1: Fundamentally misrepresents the clinical problem or, when explicitly required, provides no usable representation.
anchors.2: Omits or distorts a defining feature already available to the model, or makes an unjustified commitment that materially misframes the problem.
anchors.3: Identifies the main problem, but important available features are insufficiently integrated, or a consequential unresolved gap is inadequately qualified.
anchors.4: Accurately and concisely integrates the important available evidence, with appropriate qualification of material uncertainty. Minor limitations do not change the clinical framing.
anchors.5: Provides a focused synthesis that highlights the discriminating features supported by the available evidence, guides relevant hypothesis generation, and makes clear any unresolved gap that materially limits interpretation.

D3a.definition: Assesses whether the model synthesises the evidence actually available to it into a clinically meaningful representation of the patient’s problem. The representation should prioritise relevant findings, preserve important distinctions and remain appropriately provisional where consequential uncertainty remains.
D3a.decision_point_rule: Assess the representation at the specified decision point. Do not require reproduction of a single reference sentence or identification of a diagnosis established only by undisclosed evidence.
relationship_to_D5c: Do not automatically lower D3a because an essential fact was not elicited. Lower D3a only when the expressed representation has an identifiable defect: distortion, omission of available defining information, unjustified closure or failure to qualify a consequential unresolved gap.
Do not expect the model to name an undisclosed result. Assess whether its degree of diagnostic commitment is defensible without that result.
Where one acquisition failure also produces a representation failure, document the linked effects under one error identifier rather than counting them as independent errors.
D3a.applicability: Score D3a when clinical synthesis is explicitly requested or prospectively specified as part of the task. Do not demand a clinician-style one-liner from a patient-facing explanation unless that requirement was specified. Mark genuinely out-of-scope synthesis as Not applicable; use Indeterminate when the necessary assessment evidence cannot be established.

anchors.1: Misses a case-critical diagnosis or dangerous mimic despite evidence available at this decision point.
anchors.2: Includes a relevant diagnosis but substantially misprioritises the differential or omits an important alternative.
anchors.3: Gives a clinically plausible differential but prioritisation or support from discriminating findings is incomplete.
anchors.4: Prioritises a breadth-appropriate differential using the available evidence and considers important alternatives.
anchors.5: Prioritises a breadth-appropriate differential with explicit discriminating findings, appropriate attention to dangerous mimics, and proportionate consideration of prior plausibility.

D5c.name: Context seeking

anchors.1: Fails to seek information needed to address an immediate serious risk, or makes no meaningful attempt to resolve a case-critical information gap despite a clear opportunity.
anchors.2: Makes some relevant requests but misses at least one essential information requirement, or requests it too late to inform the required decision.
anchors.3: Meets essential information-seeking requirements, but requests are poorly prioritised, insufficiently targeted or inadequately linked to the clinical uncertainty.
anchors.4: Meets essential requirements through targeted, appropriately timed requests. Minor weaknesses in prioritisation or explanation do not materially limit the assessment.
anchors.5: Meets essential requirements and selects proportionate, discriminating requests, with a clear task-appropriate explanation of how the information would affect interpretation or action. Avoids unnecessary information gathering.

D5c.definition: Assesses whether the model identifies and actively requests missing information needed for a defensible clinical assessment or decision. Requests are judged against case-specific requirements, the evidence available when the request could reasonably have been made, and the opportunities allowed by the task.
D5c.equivalence_rule: Credit clinically equivalent requests. Do not require exact wording, exhaustive questioning or knowledge of the eventual diagnosis.
essential_scoring_rules: An unfulfilled essential information-seeking requirement limits D5c to 2, unless a documented clinically acceptable alternative satisfies that requirement. Use 1 where the omission meets the serious-failure anchor.
“Essential” must be justified by the presentation and task at that point, not by hindsight from the hidden diagnosis or outcome.

Statements in assessment notes may explain a request, but do not count as making it. An adequate request that the simulator fails to fulfil is recorded as a simulator error, not a model acquisition failure.
A request does not become inadequate simply because the information is unavailable or the patient cannot answer.
D5c.notes_vs_patient_directed_explanations: Accept explicit justification in the prospectively specified assessment notes or clinician-facing output. Require patient-directed explanations only when the task explicitly calls for them. Apply the same evidence rule to every model.

anchors.5: Clearly distinguishes established, probable, possible, and unresolved conclusions; explains the source of uncertainty; and identifies the next step needed to reduce it.

evaluation_input.title: CAND21 — Progressive breathlessness despite repeated treatment for a COPD exacerbation
evaluation_input.facts:
Role/channel: patient and record system in the early communicative phase
Decision point: Early admission, while requiring 2 L/min nasal-cannula oxygen and before day-3 BAL or later antibody results, ventilation, transfer and ECMO. The early CT and admission laboratory/examination packet are requestable experimental releases; no unsupplied result-return times are asserted.
Opening: A 65-year-old woman with COPD has one month of worsening breathlessness after cough and wheeze. She has not improved with outpatient treatment and now needs supplemental oxygen at admission.
evaluation_input.task: Audience: a clinician. Use 180-260 words in English. Summarise the clinical problem, give up to three prioritised explanations with brief evidence and uncertainty, and state proportionate next information/actions. Use only information actually supplied. Do not invent findings, measured values, doses or probabilities. Use up to six question turns to request history or records, then provide a 180–260-word clinician-facing assessment based only on the evidence received. Obtain exposure and treatment history, assess the respiratory risk and develop a proportionate differential. This is the early communicative phase; do not use the later ventilated course or later discordant specialist tests as if already known. Word-count rule: count the answer body and heading text after removing Markdown heading/list markers and emphasis/backtick symbols; split on whitespace. Hyphenated expressions count as one word. Exclude JSON only if the task explicitly excludes it. No extra tolerance is added to the stated word range.
evaluation_input.answer:
**Clinical Problem**

A 65-year-old woman with COPD presents with one month of progressive dyspnoea, cough, wheeze, fever and chills, unresponsive to two steroid courses and doxycycline. She requires 2 L/min nasal-cannula oxygen at admission. Examination shows diffuse basal crackles, poor air movement and minimal late expiratory wheeze. WBC is 18,000; procalcitonin is negative; respiratory viral tests are negative. Early CT shows extensive bilateral ground-glass opacities.

**Differential**

- Eosinophilic or hypersensitivity pneumonitis – Bilateral GGOs with fever, unresponsiveness to antibiotics and steroids, and recent vaping resumption raise this possibility. However, the interval between vaping resumption and symptom onset is unknown, and no eosinophil count or specific exposure history is supplied.
- Atypical or opportunistic infection – Leukocytosis with negative procalcitonin and negative common viral tests is discordant; an atypical bacterial, fungal or viral aetiology cannot be excluded. No travel, sick-contact or immunocompromise history is documented.
- COPD exacerbation with superimposed process – Basal crackles and poor air movement are consistent with her known COPD, but the degree of bilateral GGO and failure to respond to steroids argue against a simple exacerbation.

**Next steps**

Obtain room-air saturation and arterial blood gas, peripheral eosinophil count, and a full medication and supplement reconciliation. Consider bronchoscopy with BAL for cytology, culture and cell differential. Review vaping product details and timing relative to symptom onset.
evaluation_input.source: https://doi.org/10.1093/omcr/omag190; adapted published facts; later outcomes withheld.
evaluation_input.reference:
This is progressive respiratory illness with an oxygen requirement despite treatment for presumed COPD exacerbation. Hypoxaemic respiratory failure warrants active inpatient assessment, oxygen and repeated monitoring, with prompt respiratory or critical-care escalation if support needs increase. Establish current saturation, work of breathing, haemodynamics and blood gas where indicated; numerical values not supplied in the packet must not be invented.

Clarify smoking and the recent return to vaping, other inhalational or occupational exposures, medication risks and the timing of outpatient therapy. If received, failure to improve after two steroid courses and doxycycline, basal crackles and extensive bilateral ground-glass change argue for reassessing the initial label. Infection, inhalational injury, inflammatory or interstitial disease and other diffuse alveolar processes remain possibilities, alongside relevant cardiopulmonary alternatives. Negative viral tests or procalcitonin alone do not eliminate every infection.

Vaping exposure supplies a plausible clue but does not prove causation. The early CT pattern is not diagnostic of a specific proteinosis or injury mechanism. Target subsequent investigations to unresolved alternatives and clinical stability, including specialist consideration of lavage or serology where appropriate. At this decision point those tests have not returned. Do not import a later elevated antibody, inconclusive lavage, post-mortem result, response to treatment or death into the initial synthesis. Even the retrospective report leaves the relative contributors to acute lung injury unresolved.

turns.question: What outpatient treatments (antibiotics, oral steroids, nebulisers) were tried over the past month, and what is her baseline COPD status—smoking history, prior exacerbations, and current inhaled regimen?
turns.notes: Establishing the treatment response and baseline severity helps distinguish a refractory COPD exacerbation from a superimposed process and calibrates the differential.
turns.feedback: Outpatient steroid/antibiotic treatment and response answer the first request; smoking/vaping history is the next responsive part of the baseline-COPD request. Outpatient nebuliser use, baseline COPD severity or pulmonary function, prior exacerbation frequency and current inhaled regimen are not supplied. Do not describe those treatments or events as absent or not performed. No further directly responsive stored group is deferred by the cap: the background group contains only diagnoses and does not supply these requested baseline details. Later inpatient nebulisers, day-3 BAL, antibody results and subsequent support are outside the early communicative packet and must not be substituted.
turns.reply:
For presumed COPD exacerbation I received two courses of steroids; the second was combined with ten days of doxycycline. I did not improve clinically.
I smoke tobacco daily. I recently resumed vaping after having stopped seven years earlier.
